items.stem: What does the term ceteris paribus mean?
items.answer: All other things remaining equal
items.markingKey: Ceteris paribus: holding all other variables constant so the effect of one change can be isolated.

items.stem: Explain why economists make use of the ceteris paribus assumption when analysing demand.
items.answer: Demand depends on many variables (price, income, tastes, prices of related goods). Holding the others constant isolates the effect of one change, such as price, on quantity demanded.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: many variables affect demand; 1 mark: holding others constant isolates one effect [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength and one limitation of using economic models.
items.answer: Strength: they simplify complex reality so cause and effect can be analysed and predictions made. Limitation: assumptions may be unrealistic, so predictions may be inaccurate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: strength; 1 mark: limitation [2]

items.stem: A theory predicts that higher interest rates in Kestria will reduce borrowing; economists check this using data from the last 20 years. Which aspect of economic method does this illustrate?
items.answer: Testing a hypothesis with evidence
items.markingKey: Testing a hypothesis with evidence: the prediction is compared with real-world data.

items.stem: A theory predicts that higher interest rates in Rovania will reduce borrowing; economists check this using data from the last 20 years. Which aspect of economic method does this illustrate? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Testing a hypothesis with evidence: the prediction is compared with real-world data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Testing a hypothesis with evidence; 1 mark: explanation – the prediction is compared with real-world data. [2]

items.stem: Extract: In Ostrelia the tax on sugary drinks was raised from 8 to 10 cents per litre. Monthly sales fell from 400 million to 380 million litres. The health minister said: “This shows sugar taxes work and every country should have one.” Over the same months a large advertising campaign on healthy eating was run. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in monthly sales. (b) Identify one positive and one normative statement in the minister’s comment.
items.answer: (a) 5% (b) “Sugar taxes work” (reduce consumption) is positive/testable; “every country should have one” is normative.

items.stem: Explain why economic predictions are often less precise than predictions in physics.
items.answer: Economics studies human behaviour, which changes with expectations, culture and information; many variables change at once and controlled experiments are rarely possible.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: human behaviour unpredictable; 1 mark: cannot hold other things equal / no controlled experiments [2]

items.stem: A model of Quentara’s economy assumes that firms aim only to maximise profit. Which aspect of economic method does this illustrate?
items.answer: Simplifying assumption about behaviour
items.markingKey: Simplifying assumption about behaviour: it simplifies firms’ objectives to make the model manageable.

items.stem: The government of Esteria has asked its economic advisers for a report on this issue. Explain why economists use models and assumptions such as ceteris paribus.
items.answer: Reality is complex; models simplify to isolate relationships; ceteris paribus holds other variables constant; allows predictions and testing; examples (demand curve).
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Reality is complex; models simplify to isolate relationships; ceteris paribus holds other variables constant; allows predictions and testing; examples (demand curve). Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: What is a positive statement?
options: A statement that is always true
A statement of fact that can be tested against evidence
A statement that expresses an opinion about what ought to happen
A statement that supports government policy
items.answer: A statement of fact that can be tested against evidence
items.markingKey: Positive statements are objective and testable, whether true or false.

items.stem: Explain the difference between positive and normative statements, giving an example of each.
items.answer: Positive: objective statement that can be tested with evidence, e.g. “inflation was 3% last year”. Normative: contains a value judgement about what ought to be, e.g. “inflation should be lower”.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: positive definition; 1 mark: normative definition; 1 mark: valid examples [3]

items.stem: Explain why economists might agree on positive statements but disagree on normative statements.
items.answer: Positive statements can be settled by evidence, but normative statements depend on value judgements (e.g. about fairness), which differ between people.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: positive testable; 1 mark: normative depend on values [2]

items.stem: A newspaper report states that the unemployment rate in Valdoria rose to 6% last year. Is this statement positive or normative?
items.answer: Positive
items.markingKey: Positive: it can be tested against evidence.

items.stem: Classify each of the following statements as positive or normative and explain your choice. (i) “The average wage in Kuala Lumpur is higher than the national average.” (ii) “It is wrong that Granite Holdings pays its managers so much.”
items.answer: (i) positive (ii) normative
items.markingKey: (i) positive – testable with evidence [1] (ii) normative – value judgement [1] Total [2]

items.stem: Classify each of the following statements as positive or normative and explain your choice. (i) “Fendaria ought to spend more on healthcare than on defence.” (ii) “Increasing the minimum wage will reduce employment of young workers.” (iii) “The unemployment rate in Fendaria rose to 6% last year.”
items.answer: (i) normative (ii) positive (iii) positive
items.markingKey: (i) normative – value judgement [1] (ii) positive – testable with evidence [1] (iii) positive – testable with evidence [1] Total [3]

items.stem: Extract: In Zentara the tax on sugary drinks was raised from 12 to 15 cents per litre. Monthly sales fell from 600 million to 540 million litres. The health minister said: “This shows sugar taxes work and every country should have one.” Over the same months a large advertising campaign on healthy eating was run. (a) Identify one positive and one normative statement in the minister’s comment. (b) Explain why the evidence in the extract may not prove that the tax caused the fall in sales.
items.answer: (a) “Sugar taxes work” (reduce consumption) is positive/testable; “every country should have one” is normative. (b) Ceteris paribus did not hold: the advertising campaign also reduced demand; other factors (prices of substitutes, weather) may have changed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: other variables changed; 1 mark: link to extract [2]

items.stem: Extract: In Tarvia the tax on sugary drinks was raised from 12 to 15 cents per litre. Monthly sales fell from 500 million to 450 million litres. The health minister said: “This shows sugar taxes work and every country should have one.” Over the same months a large advertising campaign on healthy eating was run. (a) Explain why the evidence in the extract may not prove that the tax caused the fall in sales. (b) Discuss whether the effects of the tax are likely to be greater in the long run than in the short run.
items.answer: (a) Ceteris paribus did not hold: the advertising campaign also reduced demand; other factors (prices of substitutes, weather) may have changed. (b) In the long run habits change, firms reformulate drinks and substitutes appear, so the response is larger; but addiction and brand loyalty may limit it; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: other variables changed; 1 mark: link to extract [2] (b) Credit: In the long run habits change, firms reformulate drinks and substitutes appear, so the response is larger; but addiction and brand loyalty may limit it; judgement. [4]

items.stem: Explain why government policy decisions usually involve normative judgements.
items.answer: Policies create winners and losers; choosing between them requires judgements about what is fair or desirable, not only facts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: trade-offs/winners and losers; 1 mark: value judgement required [2]

items.stem: A report on Loristan states: “Youth unemployment is 18%, which is unacceptably high.” Explain which parts of this sentence are positive and which are normative.
items.answer: “Youth unemployment is 18%” is positive (testable); “unacceptably high” is normative (value judgement).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: positive part; 1 mark: normative part [2]

items.stem: A politician in Lunaria says that the price of bicycles is too high. (a) Explain why this is a normative statement. (b) Write a related positive statement that an economist could test, and state the evidence needed to test it.
items.answer: (a) It expresses an opinion/value judgement about what ought to be and cannot be proved true or false. (b) e.g. a cause-and-effect claim about the policy’s outcome (such as its effect on prices, output or employment), tested with data collected before and after the change or compared with similar places.
items.markingKey: (a) value judgement / not testable [2] (b) valid testable statement [1]; appropriate evidence [1] [2] Total [4]

items.stem: The government of Tarvia has asked its economic advisers for a report on this issue. Explain the difference between positive and normative statements and why the distinction matters in economics.
items.answer: Definitions with examples; positive testable, normative value judgements; economists can settle positive disputes with evidence; policy combines both.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Definitions with examples; positive testable, normative value judgements; economists can settle positive disputes with evidence; policy combines both. items.stem: What is meant by the short run in economics?
options: A period in which technology changes
A period in which all factors can be varied
A period in which at least one factor of production is fixed
A period of less than one year
items.answer: A period in which at least one factor of production is fixed
items.markingKey: SR: some factors fixed (e.g. capital/plant); LR: all factors variable.

items.stem: What is meant by the long run?
options: A period in which technology and all factors change
A period in which all factors of production can be varied but technology is given
A period of more than five years
A period in which at least one factor is fixed
items.answer: A period in which all factors of production can be varied but technology is given
items.markingKey: LR: all inputs variable, state of technology fixed.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the short run and the long run.
items.answer: Short run: at least one factor (usually capital) is fixed, so output can only be changed by varying other inputs. Long run: all factors can be varied, so the scale of production can change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: SR fixed factor; 1 mark: LR all factors variable [2]

items.stem: A hotel group moves out of its old building into a larger purpose-built hotel. Which time period does this change illustrate?
items.answer: Long run
items.markingKey: Long run: all factors, including buildings, are varied.

items.stem: Extract: In Merania the tax on sugary drinks was raised from 8 to 10 cents per litre. Monthly sales fell from 400 million to 360 million litres. The health minister said: “This shows sugar taxes work and every country should have one.” Over the same months a large advertising campaign on healthy eating was run. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in monthly sales. (b) Explain why the evidence in the extract may not prove that the tax caused the fall in sales.
items.answer: (a) 10% (b) Ceteris paribus did not hold: the advertising campaign also reduced demand; other factors (prices of substitutes, weather) may have changed.
items.markingKey: (a) (400 − 360)/400 × 100 [2] (b) 1 mark: other variables changed; 1 mark: link to extract [2]

items.stem: A hotel group moves out of its old building into a larger purpose-built hotel. Which time period does this change illustrate? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Long run: all factors, including buildings, are varied.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Long run; 1 mark: explanation – all factors, including buildings, are varied. [2]

items.stem: What does it mean to make a decision at the margin?
options: Comparing the extra benefit with the extra cost of one more unit
Comparing total benefit with total cost
Making a decision without considering costs
items.answer: Comparing the extra benefit with the extra cost of one more unit
items.markingKey: Marginal analysis: compare MB and MC of a small change.

items.stem: Explain why a rational decision-maker compares marginal benefit with marginal cost rather than total benefit with total cost.
items.answer: Most decisions are about doing a little more or less; comparing the extra benefit and cost of that change shows whether it raises net benefit, which totals do not show.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: decisions are about small changes; 1 mark: MB vs MC shows whether net benefit rises [2]

items.stem: Explain why a student might stop revising after four hours even though more revision would still raise the expected mark.
items.answer: The marginal benefit of each extra hour falls (fatigue) while the marginal cost (forgone leisure/sleep) rises; once MC exceeds MB, further revision reduces net benefit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: falling MB; 1 mark: rising MC/opportunity cost; 1 mark: stop where MB = MC [3]

items.stem: The table shows the marginal benefit and marginal cost of hours of tutoring for a council in Westaria. Number of hours of tutoring: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Marginal benefit ($): 70, 60, 50, 34, 22, 10; Marginal cost ($): 25, 33, 45, 49, 65, 75. How many should be provided to maximise net benefit?
items.markingKey: Provide while MB ≥ MC: unit 3 has MB 50 ≥ MC 45; unit 4 has MB 34 < MC 49.

items.stem: The table shows the marginal benefit and marginal cost of kilometres of new cycle lane for a council in Umbria Nova. Number of kilometres of new cycle lane: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Marginal benefit ($): 60, 50, 36, 24, 20, 0; Marginal cost ($): 20, 30, 40, 44, 52, 60. (a) State the quantity that maximises net benefit and explain why. (b) Calculate the total net benefit at this quantity.
items.answer: (a) 2: every unit up to 2 has MB ≥ MC; the next has MC > MB. (b) $60
items.markingKey: (a) 2 [1]; MB ≥ MC rule [1] (b) Σ(MB − MC) for units 1–2 = 60 [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: In Quentara the tax on sugary drinks was raised from 12 to 15 cents per litre. Monthly sales fell from 500 million to 460 million litres. The health minister said: “This shows sugar taxes work and every country should have one.” Over the same months a large advertising campaign on healthy eating was run. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in monthly sales. (b) Explain how the government could use marginal analysis to decide the size of the tax.
items.answer: (a) 8% (b) Raise the tax while the marginal benefit (health gains) of the lower consumption exceeds the marginal cost (lost consumer welfare, burden on the poor).
items.markingKey: (a) (500 − 460)/500 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Raise the tax while the marginal benefit (health gains) of the lower consumption exceeds the marginal cost (lost consumer welfare, burden on the poor). [2]

items.stem: Explain how marginal analysis helps a government decide how much pollution to allow.
items.answer: Reducing pollution further has a rising marginal cost and a falling marginal benefit; the optimal amount of clean-up is where the two are equal, not zero pollution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MB and MC of reduction; 1 mark: optimum where equal [2]

items.stem: The table shows the marginal benefit and marginal cost of street cleaning shifts for a council in Fendaria. Number of street cleaning shifts: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Marginal benefit ($): 70, 58, 50, 40, 22, 10; Marginal cost ($): 30, 40, 46, 60, 70, 70. (a) State the quantity that maximises net benefit and explain why. (b) Calculate the total net benefit at this quantity. (c) Explain what would happen to net benefit if 4 were provided.
items.answer: (a) 3: every unit up to 3 has MB ≥ MC; the next has MC > MB. (b) $62 (c) Net benefit falls by $20 to $42.
items.markingKey: (a) 3 [1]; MB ≥ MC rule [1] (b) Σ(MB − MC) for units 1–3 = 62 [2] (c) loss of 20 [1] Total [5]

items.stem: Why is economics described as a social science?
options: It studies human behaviour in using scarce resources, using scientific methods where possible
It can carry out controlled laboratory experiments on whole economies
items.answer: It studies human behaviour in using scarce resources, using scientific methods where possible
items.markingKey: Economics uses models, hypotheses and data, but studies people, whose behaviour varies.

items.stem: A model used by the central bank of Kestria assumes that consumers always act rationally. Explain why this assumption is made and one problem with it.
items.answer: It simplifies analysis and allows predictions; but consumers may act on habit, emotion or limited information, so the model may predict wrongly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: why assumed; 1 mark: problem [2]

items.stem: A model predicted that when the price of concert tickets in Jovania rose from $20 to $24, weekly sales would fall from 1500 to 1275 units, ceteris paribus. In fact, sales were 1530 units, and average incomes rose by 6% over the same period. Calculate the percentage change in sales predicted by the model.

A model predicted that when the price of coffee in Ostrelia rose from $50 to $55, weekly sales would fall from 1200 to 960 units, ceteris paribus. In fact, sales were 1260 units, and average incomes rose by 5% over the same period. (a) Calculate the predicted and the actual percentage changes in sales. (b) Using the idea of ceteris paribus, explain why the prediction was not accurate.
items.answer: (a) Predicted −20%; actual 5%. (b) Other things did not stay equal: higher incomes shifted demand to the right (if coffee is normal), offsetting the price effect.
items.markingKey: (a) both percentages [2] (b) ceteris paribus violated [1]; income rise shifts demand [1] [4]

items.stem: What is a normative statement?

A statement made by an economist
A statement about past events only
A statement containing a value judgement about what ought to be
items.answer: A statement containing a value judgement about what ought to be

items.stem: Two economists in Gorvania agree that a sugar tax would cut obesity by 5% but disagree about whether it should be introduced. Explain why.
items.answer: They agree on the positive (testable) effect but differ in value judgements about fairness, freedom of choice and the burden on low-income households.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: agree on positive; 1 mark: disagree on normative values [2]

items.stem: What distinguishes the very long run from the long run?
options: In the very long run technology and the institutional framework can also change
Only labour can change in the very long run
Prices are fixed in the very long run
All factors are fixed in the very long run
items.answer: In the very long run technology and the institutional framework can also change
items.markingKey: VLR: technology, laws and institutions change.

items.stem: Explain why price elasticity of supply tends to be greater in the long run than in the short run.
items.answer: In the long run firms can change all factors, build new capacity and new firms can enter, so output responds more to a price change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: more factors variable/capacity; 1 mark: greater response to price [2]

items.stem: Lumen Ltd produces 1200 units a week in one factory. Overtime can raise output by up to 20% within a month. A new production line, taking 18 months to install, would raise capacity by 60%. Calculate the maximum weekly output possible in the short run.
items.answer: 1440 units

items.stem: A bus company in Karachi has empty seats on a late-night service. Explain, using marginal analysis, why it may sell remaining seats very cheaply.
items.answer: The marginal cost of carrying one more passenger is almost zero once the bus runs, so any fare above that marginal cost adds to revenue and profit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MC of extra passenger close to zero; 1 mark: price above MC raises profit [2]

items.stem: Arjun is deciding whether to work an extra hour for Meridian Group. Explain how Arjun would make this decision at the margin.
items.answer: Compare the extra wage (marginal benefit) with the value of the leisure given up (marginal cost); work the extra hour only if the benefit is at least the cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MB = extra pay; 1 mark: MC = forgone leisure; decision rule [2]

items.stem: Why do economists use models?

To simplify reality so that relationships between variables can be analysed
To describe every detail of the real world
To make value judgements about policy
items.answer: To simplify reality so that relationships between variables can be analysed

items.stem: In a revision note Samuel wrote: ‘Economic models are useless because they are based on unrealistic assumptions.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: All models simplify; assumptions make analysis manageable, and a model is useful if it explains and predicts reasonably well, even if its assumptions are not exactly true.

items.answer: (a) 10% (b) “Sugar taxes work” (reduce consumption) is positive/testable; “every country should have one” is normative.

items.stem: Extract: In Gorvania the tax on sugary drinks was raised from 20 to 25 cents per litre. Monthly sales fell from 600 million to 552 million litres. The health minister said: “This shows sugar taxes work and every country should have one.” Over the same months a large advertising campaign on healthy eating was run. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in monthly sales. (b) Discuss whether the effects of the tax are likely to be greater in the long run than in the short run.
items.answer: (a) 8% (b) In the long run habits change, firms reformulate drinks and substitutes appear, so the response is larger; but addiction and brand loyalty may limit it; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) (600 − 552)/600 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: In the long run habits change, firms reformulate drinks and substitutes appear, so the response is larger; but addiction and brand loyalty may limit it; judgement. [4]

items.stem: Why is the length of the short run different between industries?
options: Because the short run is always six months
Because the time needed to change fixed factors such as plant differs between industries
Because governments set it by law
Because all firms use the same machinery
items.answer: Because the time needed to change fixed factors such as plant differs between industries
items.markingKey: E.g. a café can expand quickly, a power station takes years.

items.stem: Explain why the short run for a power station is much longer than for a hairdresser.
items.answer: A power station needs many years to plan and build new capacity, whereas a hairdresser can rent another chair or small premises in weeks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: time to change fixed capital differs; 1 mark: applied examples [2]

items.stem: Delta Foods asks its workers in Dubai to work overtime to meet a rise in orders. Which time period does this change illustrate?
items.answer: Short run
items.markingKey: Short run: labour is varied while the factory (capital) is fixed.

items.stem: In a revision note Kwame wrote: ‘If eating a meal gives you a lot of total satisfaction, you should always order another one.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: The decision should depend on the marginal benefit of the next meal compared with its marginal cost, not on total satisfaction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – The decision should depend on the marginal benefit of the next meal compared with its marginal cost, not on total satisfaction. [2]

items.stem: The table shows the marginal benefit and marginal cost of kilometres of new cycle lane for a council in Jovania. Number of kilometres of new cycle lane: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Marginal benefit ($): 100, 88, 80, 70, 52, 50; Marginal cost ($): 20, 28, 40, 50, 60, 60. How many should be provided to maximise net benefit?
items.markingKey: Provide while MB ≥ MC: unit 4 has MB 70 ≥ MC 50; unit 5 has MB 52 < MC 60.

items.stem: The table shows the marginal benefit and marginal cost of hours of tutoring for a council in Halvoria. Number of hours of tutoring: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Marginal benefit ($): 80, 68, 56, 44, 40, 20; Marginal cost ($): 20, 30, 36, 44, 52, 60. (a) State the quantity that maximises net benefit and explain why. (b) Calculate the total net benefit at this quantity.
items.answer: (a) 4: every unit up to 4 has MB ≥ MC; the next has MC > MB. (b) $118
items.markingKey: (a) 4 [1]; MB ≥ MC rule [1] (b) Σ(MB − MC) for units 1–4 = 118 [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: In Umbria Nova the tax on sugary drinks was raised from 8 to 10 cents per litre. Monthly sales fell from 400 million to 360 million litres. The health minister said: “This shows sugar taxes work and every country should have one.” Over the same months a large advertising campaign on healthy eating was run. (a) Explain why the evidence in the extract may not prove that the tax caused the fall in sales. (b) Explain how the government could use marginal analysis to decide the size of the tax.
items.answer: (a) Ceteris paribus did not hold: the advertising campaign also reduced demand; other factors (prices of substitutes, weather) may have changed. (b) Raise the tax while the marginal benefit (health gains) of the lower consumption exceeds the marginal cost (lost consumer welfare, burden on the poor).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: other variables changed; 1 mark: link to extract [2] (b) Credit: Raise the tax while the marginal benefit (health gains) of the lower consumption exceeds the marginal cost (lost consumer welfare, burden on the poor). [2]
